metadata.title: Planting wasabi seeds
metadata.description: Founder of Mountain Gardens, Joe Hollis demonstrates how to plant wasabi seeds. After collecting the seed from plants within the forest, Joe separates the seed from the pods using large sieves. A potting mix made of decomposed leaves and perlite is used in planting the wasabi seeds.

transcript.text: As the pods dry out

some of them will open spontaneously but the rest
need some encouragement.
So,
there's quite a bunch of seed, some more fell down here.
Get them all in one place.
It's mostly
leaf mold, rotten leaves is the basis of it
instead of peat moss and then

chipped, shredded bark that you can buy as
mulch
like Nature's Helper or something and then the white stuff is perlite which is an
expanded clay products of some kind

which is just in there to promote
drainage
and very little fertilizer... there might be a
tiny bit of bone meal in here. We don't put much fertilizer in the woodland
mix
because the woodland plants don't really need much fertilizer. There's nothing too trickey about
this.
I usually plant about

20 seeds in a pot. I think in a bigger
pot they
have a better chance of surviving to

germinate next spring as opposed to say
doing it in little six packs or something.

Then sometimes I do and sometimes I
don't
give them a topping of this stuff which is
granite grit. It's sold mainly for
poultry chickens and so on. People who raise poultry

provide grit to them and they use it in their
craw to
break up the food. So it

functions as a sort of a mulch. It keeps
the pots from drying out too fast,
helps a little bit with weeds

getting in there and in particular helps
because I'm just going to leave this pot sitting
out here
and it's not going to germinate until next spring. Well, there's

lots of thunder storms and so on so you
can get quite a lot of soil compaction
during that period of time. The soil level
will be way down here and then when you don't have any pour space, things have difficulty
growing
or even germinating, so the

the gravel helps with that - helps prevent
that
pounding rain from splattering things out
so that's how I do most of my woodland
native woodland plants.

summary.brief: Hands sift wasabi seeds, prepare a leaf‑mold soil mix, fill a pot, and plant the seeds.
summary.detailed: The video opens with title slides about forest farming and planting wasabi. Two hands use a mesh sifter to separate black wasabi seeds from debris, collecting the clean seeds in a white bowl. The demonstrator then mixes leaf‑mold (rotten leaves), perlite, a tiny amount of fertilizer or bone meal, and a pinch of granite grit, pouring the blend from a bowl into a small green plastic container on a wooden table. The soil is spread evenly, tapped lightly, and gently patted down with the palm. The hand sprinklings the sifted seeds over the surface, lightly presses them into the soil with a fingertip, and smooths the top again. The camera pulls back to show the filled pot among other labeled containers, followed by a final shot of seedlings emerging from the pot. The segment ends with informational slides displaying the USDA National Agroforestry Center and Virginia Tech logos.

action.detailed: Sift the seeds, mix leaf‑mold with perlite and a pinch of granite grit, fill the pot with the mixture, sprinkle the seeds onto the soil, and gently press and pat the soil to embed the seeds.

The hand sprinklings the sifted seeds over the surface, lightly presses them into the soil with a fingertip, and smooths the top again. The camera pulls back to show the filled pot among other labeled containers, followed by a final shot of seedlings emerging from the pot. The segment ends with informational slides displaying the USDA National Agroforestry Center and Virginia Tech logos.
